title: trataka
hook: the candle is blown out and the room goes dark: what is a steady gaze for, after that?

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka moved onto the body: the Gita's gaze at the tip of the nose and between the brows.

The sit is over. Someone leans forward and blows out the candle. A thread of smoke, the smell of wax, and the room goes dark. Then the light switch, the kitchen, the phone, the street, a crowd of things asking to be looked at. What is a steady gaze for, once the candle is out? On the last day of trataka, the Gita suggests where the gaze is meant to end up, and it isn't on a candle at all.
screen: `THE SIT IS OVER. THE FLAME IS OUT.` → `A CROWD OF THINGS ASKS TO BE SEEN.` → `WHERE IS THE GAZE MEANT TO END UP?`

segments.voice: In chapter six of the Gita, Krishna describes the one whose mind has become steady in yoga. In paraphrase: such a person sees the Self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self, and sees the same everywhere. The Sanskrit is sama-darshana: same-seeing, an even gaze. In the next verse, Krishna makes it personal. Whoever sees me everywhere, and sees everything in me, I am not lost to them, and they are not lost to me. So the steady gaze isn't the end. It's training for a different kind of seeing. On a flame, the eyes learn to stop jumping. Here, the steadiness goes out into the world. The same evenness looks at a stranger, a sister, a sparrow, someone difficult, and doesn't swing from wanting to pushing away. Two verses later, Krishna gives that evenness a heart. In paraphrase: the one who, by the measure of one's own self, sees pleasure or pain in every being as the same, that yogi is held to be the highest. Shankara reads it plainly: as pain is unwelcome to me, so it is to every being. An even gaze isn't a cold one. Now the seven days, in one breath: a small mark, a windless lamp, eyes turned around, a mind tied to one place, a gaze that is met, a point carried on the body, and today, a gaze that stops picking favorites. In this arc, the flame was never the goal. It was a place for the eyes to learn to be still, so they could look at the world with the same calm.
screen: `THE SELF IN ALL, ALL IN THE SELF.` · `SAMA-DARSHANA: AN EVEN GAZE.` · `I AM NOT LOST TO THEM.` · `SEVEN DAYS: FROM A MARK TO THE WORLD.` · then, large: `ONE SMALL POINT, THEN EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Rest the gaze on one small point, a flame or a mark, for a little while, blinking when you need to. Then let the gaze soften and widen, without moving the eyes, until it takes in the whole room, and look at all of it with the same calm you gave the point. If the mind starts sorting, liking this, disliking that, come back to the point, then widen again.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point, practiced, the Gita suggests, until the eyes can rest on everything with the same calm.
Your line: one small point, then everything. Tomorrow, the hands. That's day one thousand thirty-two.

howItsDone: Some teachers of meditation in Hindu traditions present single-pointed gazing as a beginning, with the Gita's ideal of seeing the same Self in all beings as where the steadiness leads.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sama-darshana, same-seeing, an even gaze. In the Gita, the one steady in yoga sees the same everywhere.

chat.says: Doesn't seeing everyone the same mean you stop caring who's hurting?
options: No. Krishna says to feel others' pain as your own; even isn't cold.
Yes. An even gaze means treating every person like a stranger.
Yes. It means caring only for those who walk the same path.
chat.meaning: In the Gita, the yogi sees others' pleasure or pain by the measure of their own. Shankara: as pain is unwelcome to me, so to every being.
